tour.title: Old Canton
tour.summary: Two centuries of the China trade in one day: colonial arcades on Shamian Island, the Qingping herbal market, the Chen Clan Academy, Beijing Road's layered high street, a granite Gothic cathedral, and one honest metro hop to the Canton Tower at night.
tour.overviewText:
Step off the high-speed train from Hong Kong and within the hour you can be eating the best dumpling of your life in the city that invented it. This walk is your way through the Guangzhou that made that dumpling possible.

Guangzhou matters because for a century it was China's only open door. Canton is simply the old English name for this same city, and from 1757 to 1842 the Canton System — the emperor's rule that all foreign trade must pass through this one port — made it the single point where China met the world. British, American and other merchants bought tea, silk and porcelain here through licensed Chinese firms, and the fortunes piled up on both sides until they didn't: Britain wanted to sell opium, China refused, and the Opium Wars followed, fought over the drug trade and free access to Chinese markets, ending with Hong Kong ceded to Britain and more ports forced open. Supporters of the old order called it free trade; Chinese histories call it humiliation; both facts sit in the stones you will walk past, and this tour states them and moves on. What survived intact is pride: Cantonese — the southern Chinese language spoken here, with its own opera, slang and nine tones — and Cantonese food, which the locals will tell you, correctly, runs China. Yum cha, the slow morning ritual of tea with small dim sum dishes, meaning bite-sized dumplings and buns, was born in teahouses like the ones on this route. Money today comes from the Pearl River Delta around you, the factory belt that makes a large share of the world's electronics, clothes and toys — the port grew rich on trade and stayed rich on manufacturing.

The shape of the walk is a loop through the old west with a metro hop east at the end. You start among the colonial arcades of Shamian Island, cross into the herbal market and the great clan academy, ride to the ancient high street and the stone cathedral, then metro to the river for the tower after dark.

Late November is Guangzhou at its kindest: dry, around 15 to 22 degrees, light jacket weather, dusk falling early enough that the tower lights come on while you still have energy. Money is RMB, meaning yuan, the Chinese currency also written CNY — park notes of small bills for market stalls, since the big sights take phones and cards. Start around 09:00 with an empty stomach; the dumplings are not optional.

Eat first, judge later. Old Canton rewards the hungry.
tour.difficulty: Easy to moderate. About 3.5 km of flat walking plus three short metro rides; crowded market aisles at Qingping, steps and thresholds at the academy and cathedral, and long standing queues at the tower in the evening.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 09:00. Late November is dry and mild, roughly 15 to 22 degrees. Do the old-west stops in daylight, ride east at dusk, and finish at the tower after dark when it is lit.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Individual credits appear under each stop's photograph.

stops.name: Shamian Island Arcades
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open island streets and parks. No ticket; the small museums and churches on the island keep their own hours. Verify locally.
stops.openingHours: Open access daily. The island is prettiest and quietest before 10:00; the churches open for services and limited visiting hours.
stops.accessibility: Mostly flat with wide pavements, but historic kerbs are high and dropped crossings are patchy. The old buildings themselves have steps at every door.
stops.insiderTip: Look up at the covered walkways, not just the facades: the arcade arches run unbroken for whole blocks, and each nation's former concession built its stretch in a slightly different style.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the island by the eastern bridge onto Shamian Street, then walk north east about 1.2 km, roughly 18 minutes, following the signs to Qingping Market. The covered herbal halls are unmissable.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Rutger van der Maar, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Walk under the banyan trees and the street turns European without asking permission. You are on Shamian Island, a green wedge in the Pearl River that Britain and France took as their concession — a slice of a Chinese city governed by foreigners — after the Opium Wars of the 1840s to 1860s, those wars fought over Britain's opium trade and forced access to Chinese ports.

The building type around you is the lesson. These are arcade houses, called qilou in Cantonese: shophouses with a covered walkway on the ground floor so pedestrians stay dry in the subtropical rain. The form is southern Chinese, but here it wears stone facades, verandas and church spires, because the island's traders rebuilt it in their own image. Consulates, banks, a church for the British and one for the French — two empires facing each other across lawns, doing business with a China they could see from their windows but governed from gunboats.

Read it the way the tour asks you to hold two thoughts. The lawns are genuinely lovely, and the architecture is genuinely fine. It is also the physical footprint of an unequal deal, built while the rest of Guangzhou crowded behind walls. Both are true, and neither needs your verdict.

No ticket, open streets, best before 10:00. When the shade tempts you to linger, leave by the eastern bridge and walk north east about 1.2 km, roughly 18 minutes, to the covered herbal halls of Qingping Market.

stops.name: Qingping Market
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open market halls; browsing is free. Prices are in RMB, meaning yuan (CNY). Haggle politely and compare two stalls before buying medicine.
stops.openingHours: Market halls open daily, roughly 08:00 to 18:00, liveliest in the morning. Verify locally as hall hours shift.
stops.accessibility: Crowded narrow aisles, wet floors in the produce halls, and steps between halls. Not step free and hard going for wheels.
stops.insiderTip: Find the dried-goods aisles — trays of scorpions, seahorses and bark next to the ginseng — and ask a seller what each thing treats. You will get a free education in Cantonese food-as-medicine.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is a metro hop, not a walk: the academy is 3.0 km north, over forty minutes on foot through heavy traffic, so do not stroll it. Walk 10 minutes to Huangsha metro station, ride Line 1 two stops west to Chen Clan Academy station, and follow the signs to the academy gate. Allow about 25 minutes door to door.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Vmenkov, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Follow your nose north off the island and the street turns into a pharmacy the size of a neighbourhood. This is Qingping Market, Guangzhou's great traditional medicine and produce bazaar, running since the late 1970s on a site traders used for far longer.

The trays are the lesson. Dried scorpions, seahorses, bark, roots, ginseng by the armful — this is Cantonese food-as-medicine, the belief that what you eat tunes the body the way a cook tunes a broth. A warming root for a cold constitution, a cooling tea for the damp heat. Whether or not you buy the pharmacology, buy the economics: this market is where the Pearl River Delta's appetite meets Yunnan's mountainsides and the South China Sea, priced in RMB, the yuan (CNY), by sellers who can tell the province of a mushroom at a glance. Browsing is free; compare two stalls before you believe any price.

One honest footnote. Qingping's wildlife stalls have drawn international criticism, and the trade in some wild species is now restricted. Notice what is labelled farmed, what is absent that older guidebooks mention, and draw your own line — the market is negotiating with its critics in real time.

When the smells have educated you enough, do not walk to the next stop. The academy is 3.0 km north, over forty minutes on foot through heavy traffic. Walk 10 minutes to Huangsha station, ride Line 1 two stops west to Chen Clan Academy station, and follow the signs. Allow about 25 minutes door to door.

stops.name: Chen Clan Academy
stops.entranceFeeNote: Ticketed museum: about ¥25 (CNY) at last check. Verify prices at the gate; Chinese museums revise them.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly 08:30 to 17:30, last entry earlier. Verify locally.
stops.accessibility: Stone thresholds at every hall door and steps between courtyards. The courtyards themselves are level once you are over the sills; not step free.
stops.insiderTip: Stand in the main courtyard and look at the roof ridges first: the procession of tiny pottery figures tells whole opera stories, and the guides at the door will decode your favourite scene.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is a metro hop, not a walk: Beijing Road is 4.3 km east, over an hour on foot, so do not stroll it. Take Line 1 from Chen Clan Academy station two stops east to Gongyuanqian, exit north, and walk 10 minutes to the pedestrian street. Allow about 25 minutes door to door.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Eduardo M. C., CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Step over the high stone threshold — lift your feet, every visitor does the same little hop — and you are inside the grandest family school in southern China. This is the Chen Clan Academy, built in the 1890s by seventy-two Chen families pooling money to lodge their sons for the imperial examinations.

A clan academy needs one breath of unpacking. In old China your surname was your welfare state: the Chens taxed themselves to house, feed and tutor boys from their villages while the boys studied the Confucian classics for the civil-service exams, the tests that chose the empire's officials. Pass, and the whole clan rose. So the building is an advertisement for what study buys: carved brick, ironwork, and the famous Shiwan pottery roof ridges — processions of tiny glazed figures acting out opera scenes above your head. The ticket runs about ¥25, meaning twenty-five yuan (CNY), but verify at the gate.

The punchline is upstairs in the craft. After the exams died with the empire in 1905, the academy became a museum of the very skills that built it: ivory carving, embroidery, woodwork. The sons stopped memorising classics; the craftsmen kept carving. Education changed its subject and the building barely noticed.

Mind the thresholds between every hall — stone sills, steps between courtyards, not step free. When you leave, do not walk east: Beijing Road is 4.3 km away, over an hour on foot. Ride Line 1 two stops east to Gongyuanqian, exit north, and walk 10 minutes to the pedestrian street. Allow about 25 minutes door to door.

stops.name: Beijing Road Pedestrian Street
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open pedestrian street. No ticket; shops and snack stalls price in RMB (CNY). Verify food prices as you go — the street is honest but tourist-priced at the centre.
stops.openingHours: Open access daily. Shops roughly 10:00 to 22:00; the street is liveliest from late afternoon into the evening.
stops.accessibility: Flat, wide, paved and step free along its length. Crowds are dense at weekends; mornings are the calm window.
stops.insiderTip: Find the glass panels set into the pavement mid-street: beneath them lie the actual Tang, Song and Ming road surfaces, stacked like pages, eleven layers deep.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk south from the pedestrian street about 2.3 km, roughly 35 minutes, following Huifu and Yide Roads toward the river. The twin granite spires rising over the rooftops are the cathedral.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Wpcpey, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
You come up out of the metro and the street is doing what it has done for a thousand years: selling everything. Beijing Road is Guangzhou's old high street, and the glass panels set into the pavement mid-street prove it — look down through them at the buried road surfaces, Tang over Song over Ming, eleven layers of shopfront street stacked under your shoes.

The mechanism is continuity with amnesia. The same strip sold goods when the Canton System — the rule that all foreign trade must pass through this one port — funnelled the world's silver through this city, and it sells phone cases and milk tea today. Names changed, dynasties fell, the Japanese occupied the city in the war, the factories rose across the delta — and the street kept its job through all of it. Browsing is free, prices in RMB (yuan), and the snack stalls halfway down are your lunch: rice rolls, wonton noodles, egg tarts, eaten standing like a local.

Stop at the covered section and look at the arcade fronts again — qilou, those covered walkways you met on Shamian, in their native habitat this time, built by Chinese merchants for Chinese shoppers. The concession borrowed the form from streets like this one, not the other way round.

Flat, paved and step free, but dense at weekends. When you have eaten, walk south about 2.3 km, roughly 35 minutes via Huifu and Yide Roads toward the river. The twin granite spires ahead are the cathedral.

stops.name: Sacred Heart Cathedral
stops.entranceFeeNote: Entry is free; donations welcome. Visiting is restricted during Mass and services — check the board at the door and verify locally.
stops.openingHours: Open daily for visiting outside service times, roughly morning to late afternoon. Closed to tourists during Mass; verify locally.
stops.accessibility: Steps up to the west door and a high threshold; the nave floor is level once inside. No step-free entrance at last check.
stops.insiderTip: Run your hand along the outside wall: every block is granite, and the mortar is said to be mixed with sticky rice — the same recipe as the old city wall.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is the last metro hop, not a walk: the tower is 6.6 km east, over ninety minutes on foot, so do not stroll it. Walk 10 minutes to Haizhu Square station, ride Line 2 to Changgang, change to Line 8 one stop to Canton Tower station, and follow the river exit. Allow about 35 minutes door to door.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Windmemories, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Turn the corner and France lands in front of you in solid granite. This is the Sacred Heart Cathedral, locally the Stone House, raised by French missionaries from the 1860s and finished in 1888 — one of the few all-granite Gothic churches anywhere on earth.

The stones carry the argument of the whole walk. Catholic missionaries had worked in China for centuries, but this cathedral rose under the protection of the unequal treaties — the deals imposed after the Opium Wars that forced ports open and sheltered foreign missions. Supporters called it religious freedom arriving; Chinese critics called it faith delivered by gunboat. Touch the wall: granite blocks, every one, set in mortar said to be mixed with sticky rice. The congregation today is Chinese and full on Sundays, which complicates every easy story about foreign impositions. Entry is free, donations welcome, but tourists are kept out during Mass — check the board, keep your voice down, skip the flash near anyone praying.

Steps at the west door and a high threshold; the nave is level once you are in. When you leave, do not walk east. The tower is 6.6 km away, over ninety minutes on foot. Walk 10 minutes to Haizhu Square, ride Line 2 to Changgang, change to Line 8 to Canton Tower station. Allow about 35 minutes door to door.

stops.name: Canton Tower Riverside
stops.entranceFeeNote: The riverside promenade is free. Ascending the tower is ticketed, about ¥150 (CNY) at last check with higher prices for the top decks. Verify at the gate; evening queues can exceed an hour.
stops.openingHours: Promenade open access daily. Tower roughly 09:30 to 22:30; verify locally. Come after dark for the lights.
stops.accessibility: Flat riverside promenade, step free and kind to wheels. The tower itself has lifts but involves long standing queues and security checks.
stops.insiderTip: Skip the paid deck if the queue is brutal: the free promenade across the river at Haixinsha gives you the tower, the new-town skyline and the light show in one frame.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Linger for the light show, then take Line 3 or the APM from Canton Tower station back toward the centre. In late November the river breeze turns sharp after 21:00 — keep the jacket you brought.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Daniel Lu, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Cross the river exit and look up until your neck complains. The Canton Tower twists 600 metres into the night sky, its waist pinched like an hourglass, lit in colours that change by the hour. Finished in 2010 for the Asian Games, it is the exclamation mark on the new Guangzhou.

Read it against everything you walked through. The old city sold tea through one port; this skyline sells everything through a delta of factories, ports and trading apps. Zhujiang New Town — the forest of glass across the water — rose from farmland in twenty years, and the tower is its flag. Supporters call it the miracle of reform; critics note the villages and arcade streets cleared to pour it. The promenade under your feet is free; the ride up costs about ¥150 (yuan) at last check, higher for the top decks, with evening queues that can exceed an hour — verify at the gate. If the line is brutal, stay where you are: the free bank at Haixinsha frames tower, skyline and light show in one photograph.

The promenade is flat and step free, the kindest ground of the day. In late November the breeze turns sharp after 21:00, so keep your jacket on.

End of the walk. You started under banyan trees where foreigners once governed a river island, and you finish under a tower the whole delta paid for. Same river, same trading city, two centuries apart — and somewhere in between, the best dumpling of your trip. Go back for seconds.
